newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition challenges govt budget in court.
newsitem.headline: German opposition challenges govt budget in court.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Wednesday they planned to file a complaint with the Constitutional Court to challenge alleged government violations in preparing its 1996 budget.
The suit would have no impact on plans for the 1998 budget now in parliamentary deliberation, but any court ruling could be an embarrassment for embattled Finance Minister Theo Waigel.

Rudolf Scharping, SPD parliamentary leader, told Germany's Southwest Radio that in preparing the budget for 1996 the government mislead parliament and violated the constitution by allowing the deficit to be higher than public investment.
"We are going to file a constitutional complaint," he said.
"The point is that the government already knew when it was planning the 1996 budget that new borrowing would exceed federal investment. That is against the constitution."
The SPD allegation is based on a study by constitutional expert Dieter Birk of Muenster University, who alleges Bonn's 1996 budget was in violation of constitutional rules.
Scharping said the federal deficit at the end of 1996 was 78.3 billion marks and investment 61 billion marks.

Separately, parliamentary deputies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition late on Tuesday approved changes to the government's tax reform bill, virtually ensuring its passage in the lower house later this week.

The changes agreed by Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP) include a number of last-minute modifications to corporate tax rules that have sparked a storm of protest from German industry.
"Ninety percent of companies are not affected by the new rules," said FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms in defence of the measures.

The most controversial changes are a new rule making it more difficult for companies to reduce tax liability by carrying forward losses from previous years and introduction of a tax on hidden reserves for power utilities.

The changes met some opposition among pro-business FDP deputies, but the FDP parliamentary group as a whole still approved the bill in a run-up vote ahead of Thursday's official vote in the lower house of parliament.
Deputies from Kohl's Christian Democrats also questioned the changes affecting how a company handles losses, but they, too, approved the modifications in the end.
Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the Federation of German Industry, told Reuters that the changes were a populist move that would make it harder for German companies to compete.
"If this package is implemented things will get much worse," he said.

He said the changes would particularly hit companies that have counted on being able to carry forward losses, such as those who invested in eastern Germany, foreign investors and new companies who tend to run up losses in the beginning.

"We are very disappointed and deeply worried about how things are developing," he said. "It seems the ruling coalition is in a battle with the opposition to see who can put forward the most populist tax proposal."
Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier, finance expert for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), told the business daily Handeslblatt that protests from German industry were understandable.
The SPD is expected to block the tax bill from final passage when the opposition-controlled upper house of parliament votes on the bill on July 4.
Matthaeus-Maier said there were several points on which a compromise with the government could be reached, including the entry-level tax rate and the level of tax-free income.

The SPD parliamentary group on Tuesday also approved a draft bill that aims to lower supplementary wage costs by cutting social security payments by two percentage points. The payments include contributions to unemployment insurance, as well as health and pension insurance.
In order to pay for the cut in unit wage costs, the SPD proposed to raise petrol taxes by six pfennigs per litre.
-- william.boston@reuters.com (Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150)
